answer.rationale: Constraints dominate: 14 days to expiry, 94% of committed volume with no buffer, and a hard 18% spend cut. Only one decision fits this cycle, and any action that physically moves material creates qualification, tooling and first-article risk inside a two-week window with no slack — so switch_primary_vendor and add_second_source are structurally wrong now even though memory_c2 and memory_c3 report good outcomes for them. memory_c5's defer worked on a NON-critical, month-to-month service; this contract is critical and does not auto-renew, so deferring is not a lever, it is an outage. That leaves renew_incumbent (memory_c1: stability, but no cost movement, which fails the 18% mandate) versus negotiate_terms (memory_c4: benchmarking moved the incumbent on price and terms; memory_c6: longer term unlocked volume pricing without narrowing scope). Negotiation captures cost while leaving the physical supply chain untouched, so delivery risk stays flat — the only path that serves both halves of the objective. I want the archive on memory_c2 because it is the most load-bearing temptation here: 'cut unit cost sharply' is exactly what the 18% mandate wants, but the record is summarized, dated 'last year', and says nothing about whether onboarding happened with a buffer, at what volume, or on which component class; if that switch was executed with slack in the line, the summary does not transfer to a 94% utilization state. I want memory_c4 because it is the basis of my intended action and I need to know what leverage actually moved the incumbent (a credible alternate quote? volume? a real walk-away?) — if the leverage was a genuine ability to switch, then my negotiation is weaker now that switching is time-infeasible, and I should expect less than 18% from price alone. Value risk to flag downstream: an 18% cut pursued through a single contract negotiation invites the supplier to concede on headline price while quietly narrowing scope, stretching lead times, or degrading incoming quality — cost recorded as saved, risk transferred into the line. memory_c6 explicitly notes scope was NOT narrowed there, so scope integrity must be an written term, not an assumption. I will scope this as a standard negotiation on the full contract but structure it guarded: hold the term short enough to preserve optionality unless multi-year volume pricing is verified, keep scope, lead time and quality obligations explicit and measured, and treat any residual gap to 18% as an open item for the next review rather than forcing it out of one supplier. Genuine uncertainty remains: I do not know whether negotiation alone reaches 18%, and dual-sourcing (memory_c3) likely remains the right structural answer once the line has buffer — this cycle's decision should not foreclose it.
